speaker: narrator
text: Christmas morning, 1914.

speaker: narrator
text: In a few seconds, this man will walk toward the German guns.

speaker: narrator
text: Unarmed. Across the ground where men had been dying for a few yards of mud.

speaker: narrator
text: That Christmas, thousands of soldiers on both sides did the same.

speaker: narrator
text: This is the day the war stopped, along parts of the Western Front. How it began, with a song. And how it ended.

speaker: narrator
text: The war had begun in August. Everyone said it would be over by Christmas.

speaker: narrator
text: By December it had dug itself into the ground: one line of trenches, from the North Sea to Switzerland.

speaker: narrator
text: Here, in Flanders, the two sides sat close enough to hear each other cough.

speaker: narrator
text: Mud to the knee. Water in every boot. A sniper waiting for one careless head.

speaker: narrator
text: Private Thomas Hale had read the same line every night for a week.

speaker: char_thomas_hale
text: Home by Christmas, she says. Didn't say which one.

speaker: char_sgt_harris
text: Keep your head down, and you might see one.

speaker: narrator
text: In early December, the Pope asked for a Christmas truce. The appeal failed. No official truce was agreed. Nobody asked the men in the trenches.

speaker: narrator
text: At Christmas, parcels came up the line. British soldiers opened brass tins from Princess Mary: cigarettes, tobacco, a Christmas card.

speaker: narrator
text: On the German side, little Christmas trees had come up the line. As night fell, they went up on the parapets, candles and all.

speaker: narrator
text: Gefreiter Friedrich Brandt had carried this photograph since August.

speaker: char_friedrich_brandt
text: Stille Nacht, heilige Nacht...

speaker: char_sgt_harris
text: What are they singing?

speaker: char_thomas_hale
text: Silent Night. Same tune as ours.

speaker: char_sgt_harris
text: Let 'em sing. Heads down.

speaker: char_thomas_hale
text: Silent night... holy night...

speaker: char_friedrich_brandt
text: Good, English! More!

speaker: narrator
text: And for the first time in months, the sound crossing no man's land was not gunfire.

speaker: narrator
text: Christmas morning came white and still.

speaker: char_friedrich_brandt
text: English! Merry Christmas!

speaker: char_sgt_harris
text: It's a trick. Nobody move.

speaker: char_friedrich_brandt
text: No shooting! Merry Christmas!

speaker: char_sgt_harris
text: Thomas! Get back down!

speaker: char_thomas_hale
text: If they wanted us dead, we'd be dead.

speaker: narrator
text: In places, the lines were only fifty yards apart. Fifty yards of frozen mud, wire, and the men who never made it back.

speaker: char_friedrich_brandt
text: You are English?

speaker: char_thomas_hale
text: And you're German?

speaker: char_friedrich_brandt
text: Saxon. Fritz, to my friends. Merry Christmas, Tommy.

speaker: char_thomas_hale
text: We're all Tommies to you. It's really my name.

speaker: narrator
text: Up and down this part of the line, the same thing was happening. Nobody had ordered it.

speaker: narrator
text: Along the British line in Flanders, it spread from trench to trench, in patches.

speaker: narrator
text: Nobody counted them. The usual estimate is that about a hundred thousand men took part.

speaker: narrator
text: They traded cigarettes, food, buttons. In a few places, accounts describe men kicking a ball around.

speaker: char_thomas_hale
text: Where'd you learn English?

speaker: char_friedrich_brandt
text: London. I was a waiter. Four years.

speaker: narrator
text: Many Germans had worked in Britain before the war. One Briton found his old barber among them, and sat down for a haircut.

speaker: char_friedrich_brandt
text: You have a family?

speaker: char_thomas_hale
text: My mum. And a little sister.

speaker: char_friedrich_brandt
text: My wife. My daughter. She is three.

speaker: char_thomas_hale
text: She looks happy.

speaker: char_friedrich_brandt
text: She thinks I am home for Christmas.

speaker: char_thomas_hale
text: So does mine.

speaker: narrator
text: But the day was not only for trading. Both sides went out to bring in their dead.

speaker: narrator
text: Some had lain out there for weeks.

speaker: char_thomas_hale
text: What was his name?

speaker: char_friedrich_brandt
text: Karl. He sang the loudest.

speaker: char_thomas_hale
text: I'm sorry.

speaker: narrator
text: At one burial, a Scottish chaplain read the Twenty-Third Psalm. A German student read it after him, in German.

speaker: narrator
text: By late afternoon, the light was going.

speaker: char_friedrich_brandt
text: Tommy... why are we fighting?

speaker: char_thomas_hale
text: I don't know.

speaker: char_friedrich_brandt
text: They told us you were the enemy.

speaker: char_thomas_hale
text: They told us the same about you.

speaker: char_friedrich_brandt
text: Tomorrow, maybe, we are enemies again.

speaker: char_thomas_hale
text: Maybe. But not today.

speaker: char_thomas_hale
text: Something to remember me by.

speaker: char_friedrich_brandt
text: Then take one of mine.

speaker: narrator
text: The sun went down on Christmas Day. Neither of them moved to leave.

speaker: narrator
text: The next morning, the men drifted back to their own trenches.

speaker: char_friedrich_brandt
text: Good luck, Tommy.

speaker: char_thomas_hale
text: You too, Fritz.

speaker: char_sgt_harris
text: Stand to.

speaker: narrator
text: At Houplines, on Boxing Day morning, a British captain ended it politely: shots into the air.

speaker: narrator
text: There had been no treaty. In some places the truce lasted hours. In others, it held until the New Year.

speaker: narrator
text: Thomas wrote home that night. So did many others. In January, British newspapers printed their letters.

speaker: narrator
text: Their commanders moved to prevent it from happening again. A few small truces still occurred in 1915, but nothing on that scale.

speaker: narrator
text: The war went on for almost four more years.
